# Resources for tidytext (Text Mining with R) {#sec-tidytext}

::: {.callout-note title="Why this matters"}
The dataset is mostly free text. @sec-mongodb-connect already walks through
tokenising, TF-IDF, sentiment, and word co-occurrence — this chapter is
where to go for more depth or techniques it doesn't cover.
:::

## The core reference

- **[Text Mining with R](https://www.tidytextmining.com/)** by Julia Silge
  and David Robinson (free, by the `tidytext` package authors). Relevant
  chapters:
  - Ch. 1 — the tidy text format (`unnest_tokens()`)
  - Ch. 2 — sentiment analysis
  - Ch. 3 — word/document frequency (tf-idf)
  - Ch. 4 — n-grams and word correlations
  - Ch. 6 — topic modeling
- `?tidytext::unnest_tokens`, `?tidytext::bind_tf_idf`, or
  `vignette(package = "tidytext")` for the function reference.

## If you want to find latent themes: topic modeling (LDA)

```r
library(topicmodels)

dtm <- tokens_clean |>
  count(report_number, word) |>
  cast_dtm(report_number, word, n)

lda_model <- LDA(dtm, k = 5, control = list(seed = 1234))

tidy(lda_model, matrix = "beta") |>   # word probabilities per topic
  group_by(topic) |>
  slice_max(beta, n = 10)
```

`tidy()` converts the model back into a tidy data frame so the rest of your
`dplyr`/`ggplot2` pipeline still applies. See Text Mining with R, Ch. 6.

## If word variants are diluting your counts: stemming

```r
library(SnowballC)

tokens_clean <- tokens_clean |>
  mutate(word_stem = wordStem(word))
```

Use deliberately, not automatically — stemming can hurt readability in a
report meant for human judges.

## If you want more corpus-linguistics tooling: `quanteda`

[`quanteda`](https://quanteda.io/) is an alternative to `tidytext`, with
built-in keyword-in-context (`kwic()`) and document-feature matrix tools.
Pick one framework and stay consistent through your analysis.

## Visualizing results

- `ggplot2::geom_col()` / `geom_point()` for frequency and tf-idf charts.
- `wordcloud2` for a quick visual summary — pair with an actual frequency
  table, since word clouds are weak for precise comparisons.
- `ggraph` + `igraph` on `widyr::pairwise_cor()` output for word-correlation
  networks.

## Cheat sheet

Posit's [tidytext cheat
sheet](https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/tidytext.pdf) — one page,
covers tokenisation, sentiment, tf-idf. Keep it open during the event.

## Keep it in scope

Text mining is a means to an analytical insight, not the insight itself. A
clear tf-idf or sentiment analysis tied to a specific question scores better
than a kitchen-sink pipeline with no narrative tying it together.
